# One Component, Many Widths
## Breakpoints and library boundaries in Figma design systems

This guide answers two questions that get confused with each other.

The first is about **width**: how should a single component behave as the screen changes size, and where should that behaviour live? The second is about **seams**: how many component libraries should you have, and what decides the boundaries between them?

They feel related because both involve the word "mobile", and because the same conversation often slides from one to the other without anyone noticing. They are not related. A breakpoint is a width. A library boundary is a technical and organisational seam, and the things that push a seam open have nothing to do with screen size. The two questions meet at exactly one place, the token layer, and Part Two says so when it gets there.

Part One is what you consult while building a component. Part Two is what you consult when somebody proposes a new library. Read Part One if you have one library and want to know how far it stretches. Read both, in order, if you are deciding the shape of a system from scratch.

Sources are weighted toward what systems ship and say about themselves: official documentation, published kits, repositories and issue threads. Practitioner essays appear as commentary and are labelled where used.

---

# Part One: Breakpoints

## The question underneath the question

Every design system has to put responsive behaviour somewhere. There are only four places it can go: into auto layout, into token values that change by mode, into variant properties on a component, or into a second component with a different name. Nobody disputes that list. What systems disagree about is the order they reach for those four, and how far down the list they get before they stop.

![Four stepped rows labelled auto layout, variable modes, variant axis and separate component, with a rising cost indicator](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*The four mechanisms, ordered by how much they duplicate. Dots on the right indicate relative maintenance cost. Most components should stop at the first or second row.*

That ordering has almost nothing to do with how responsive design works in code. A CSS media query is free. A Figma variant is not: it is duplicated geometry that a person maintains, and in an ordinary design file, a person has to switch by hand. Figma does have a mechanic that inserts the right variant for the right breakpoint automatically, matching breakpoint names against variant property values, but it lives only in Figma Sites, which as of August 2026 is still in open beta. Everywhere else, a "Mobile" variant sits in a dropdown waiting to be chosen.

That fact is usually presented as a reason to avoid breakpoint variants. It is more interesting than that, and we come back to it in Chapter 2, because the surface where that mechanic does exist is exactly the surface where breakpoint variants make the most sense.

## Chapter 1: Two problems wearing one word

Before any of the four mechanisms can be judged, there is a distinction most published guidance skips, and skipping it is why the guidance so often feels wrong in practice.

![Left, three cards reflowing from a row into a column. Right, a hero whose image and text swap position and proportion](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Left: the same parts rearranged by available width, with nothing decided. Right: a different composition that a person chose. Both get called responsive design.*

In product UI, responsiveness is **reflow**. A container of unknown width holds data of unknown length, and the layout absorbs it. Three cards in a row become three cards in a column. Nobody decided that; it fell out of the constraints. Nobody art-directs a settings page at 768 pixels.

On a marketing page, responsiveness is **art direction**. The desktop hero and the mobile hero are not the same composition at different widths. They are two compositions, and a person chose both. The image moved above the headline, the eyebrow was dropped, the button went full width, the background crop changed. Nothing about that fell out of a constraint.

Almost every well-known piece of design system writing on this topic is about the first case, because almost every well-known design system is a product system. The advice that follows, that breakpoint variants are a smell and auto layout should do the work, is correct for reflow and actively wrong for art direction. Adobe's team draws this line explicitly when explaining why Adobe.com needed a second system: marketing content is fast, fluid and content-heavy, and the patterns that provide clarity inside a product are, in their words, too subtle for the information hierarchies of marketing pages.

The next two chapters take the two cases in turn. Nearly every answer flips between them.

## Chapter 2: Product UI, where reflow is the job

Adobe Spectrum is the clearest protagonist for the token-mode approach, partly because Spectrum does not frame it as a breakpoint problem at all. Spectrum defines two platform scales for the whole system, one for cursor input and one for touch, and expresses them as a dimension with modes named `desktop` and `mobile` (the older internal names, still visible in the token data, are `medium` and `large`). The same component token then resolves differently by scale.

![Three Spectrum token names with two columns of values, desktop and mobile](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Spectrum's scale dimension. The component is not duplicated; the values it reads are. This covers padding, type and tap targets, and covers nothing where structure changes.*

There is one Button in Spectrum, not two. The touch version is the same Button read under a different scale. Salesforce arrives somewhere adjacent from a different direction, treating density as a user preference with two settings, `comfy` and `compact`, driven through spacing hooks rather than component copies.

That reframing does a lot of work, because most of what changes between a desktop layout and a phone layout is not structure, it is size. Padding grows, tap targets grow, type grows, gutters shrink. If those values live in a variable collection with modes, one component covers both. **This token layer is also the one thing Part Two will say never splits, so it is worth building carefully now.**

The cost is real, and Spectrum's own scope shows it. Scale modes change values; they do not move layers. A card whose padding grows is well served. A navigation bar that becomes a rail is not, because no amount of value substitution turns a horizontal row of five icons into a vertical column with labels. Modes were also capped at four per collection on Professional plans until late October 2025, which is why so many systems of that era ended up with variant axes instead. The limits are now 10 on Professional and 20 on Organization, which quietly changed the economics after most existing systems had already decided.

For the cases where structure genuinely changes, Material 3 shows the far end of the ladder. Material formalises five window size classes (compact below 600dp, medium to 840dp, expanded to 1200dp, then large and extra-large) and responds by swapping components outright.

![Three frames showing a bottom bar, a vertical rail and an expanded drawer, each labelled](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Material swaps navigation across window size classes. Compact gets NavigationBar, medium and expanded get NavigationRail, large gets NavigationDrawer. Three names, because they are three things.*

These are three separate components with three separate names, not three variants of a "Navigation" set, and in code they are reconciled by a scaffold that picks one. The reasoning transfers to Figma: when the anatomy, the affordances and the accessibility semantics all differ, calling them the same component is a fiction that makes both files and conversations harder.

Between those poles sits the variant axis, and its cost is arithmetic rather than philosophical.

![Thirty-two small squares beside ninety-six small squares at the same scale](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*A button with Type, State and Icon properties is already 32 variants. A three-value breakpoint axis takes it to 96. For scale, Google reduced the Material 3 list component from over 700 variants to roughly 45.*

GitLab's Pajamas offers the cautionary version of this from an adjacent problem. Pajamas removed its base components because they accumulated every possible option, leaving components full of hidden layers and properties, causing file bloat and prototype performance problems, and because removing them made updates more isolated and reduced breaking changes. Breakpoint variants fail the same way, quietly, with the pain arriving later and distributed across everyone else's files.

**The test that falls out of all this:** a product component earns a breakpoint axis when its child order or layer structure changes, not when its measurements change. By that test the qualifying list is short. Navigation. Data tables, which on narrow screens stop being tables and become stacked cards. Page headers, where actions collapse into overflow. Some modals, where a centred dialog becomes a full-screen sheet. Buttons, inputs, badges, chips, avatars and cards change size, not shape, and giving them a Desktop and Mobile variant produces two near-identical frames that drift apart the first time somebody updates one.

## Chapter 3: Marketing pages, where art direction is the job

The first thing that changes is the unit of reuse. In a product library the unit is the control: a Button, an Input, a Select. On a marketing site the unit is the **section**. Figma's own marketing team hit this early and named it: building the system behind figma.com, they componentised commonly paired elements and fully assembled sections, and called those larger organisms **FLEGOs**, a contraction of Figma and LEGO. Adobe's Consonant works the same way, with **marquees** for page headers and editorial cards as its headline components. IBM's marketing system uses **leadspace** and **content block** in its several variations.

None of those words appear in a product design system. Hold onto that, because Part Two treats it as the single easiest signal that a seam has opened.

![A page frame composed of stacked section blocks, with one section expanded into desktop, tablet and mobile compositions](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*The marketing model: a page is a vertical stack of sections, and each section carries its own authored compositions. Figma Sites builds pages exactly this way, with a primary breakpoint and secondary breakpoints that only affect themselves.*

Figma Sites encodes this model directly. A page is an auto layout stack of section blocks, with a primary breakpoint (usually Desktop) and secondary breakpoints, where changes made in a secondary breakpoint affect only that breakpoint. That is per-breakpoint art direction as a first-class mechanic, precisely what the product-UI orthodoxy warns against, and it is correct here. Sites also lets text styles carry different sizing and spacing per breakpoint without variables at all, which is a marketing-shaped affordance: a hero headline that is 72px on desktop and 32px on mobile is not a token scale, it is a decision.

Which brings back the mechanic from the introduction. The breakpoint-to-variant-name matching exists only in Figma Sites. Read as product guidance that is a limitation. Read as marketing guidance it is the opposite: the one place where breakpoint variants get real automation is the one surface where breakpoint variants are the honest representation.

The market has already voted. Relume, the highest-volume commercial Figma kit for marketing sites, ships over a thousand components and its pitch is to swap the breakpoint variant and watch the content shift into place. Every component carries the axis. In a product library that would be an anti-pattern worth an audit. For landing pages it is the product.

Two further constraints shape marketing libraries in ways product libraries never face.

**The CMS is the real specification.** Adobe's Consonant team defined three artifacts for every pattern: a defined UX pattern, a design tool template, and a CMS content block, with a one-to-one relationship between the template and the block. Their stated reason is that it lets a designer mock something up confident that when authors publish it, it will match. That constraint runs backwards into Figma: your component vocabulary is dictated by what the CMS can author, not by what CSS can express. IBM's marketing system has the same shape, with an Adobe Experience Manager team maintaining page templates as a named high-priority adopter.

**Flexibility beats variants.** Because marketing pages are continually tested and rewritten, components have to bend. Consonant's editorial card is one component covering content merchandising, events and product promotion, absorbing that range through optional eyebrows, actions, product lockups, different media and aspect ratios rather than a variant per use case. Adobe also ships quick action cards separately, describing them as different organisms that may look similar but support different information and intent. That is the structural-split test from Chapter 2 applied on the axis of purpose rather than width.

So a marketing library leans on slots and instance swaps for content variety and spends its variant budget on breakpoints. A product library does the reverse. Both are right.

## Chapter 4: Naming, which stopped being cosmetic

For years this was a question about the Assets panel. It now touches three mechanics that pull in slightly different directions. Figma Sites matches breakpoint frame names to variant property values, so those values need to be the exact breakpoint names. Code Connect maps variant enums to code props, and unmapped values fail silently rather than loudly. Slash characters still build the folder structure people navigate. A name is now a UI affordance, a matching key and an API surface at once.

Two consequences. On product components, name the property for what varies rather than for the device: `Size` or `Layout` survives contact with reality better than `Device`, because the same narrow arrangement shows up on desktop inside a side panel, and nobody looks for it under a dropdown labelled Device. On marketing sections, use device or breakpoint names, and use the ones your breakpoints are actually called, because there the matching is real.

And when a component is split rather than varianted, give it a real name. Material's NavigationRail communicates something. A component called `Navigation / Mobile` communicates only that somebody ran out of ideas, and the slash-suffix habit produces libraries where half the assets panel is duplicate entries differing by one word.

## Chapter 5: What to do

**For product components**, in order. Build responsive first: auto layout, fill and hug, min and max width, wrap, every dimension bound to a token. Push pure scaling into variable modes with a scale or density collection whose modes match your real device tiers, which is usually a shorter list than your CSS breakpoints. Add a breakpoint axis only where child order or layer structure changes. Split into a separately named component where the anatomy and semantics differ. The first two steps are consensus; the threshold between the last two is judgment, grounded in Material's split and in Shopify's 2022 Polaris kit, which shipped a small-screen toggle for exactly this class of component. Worth noting that Shopify's choice predates Figma variables entirely, so they chose from a shorter menu than you have.

**For marketing sections**, differently. Build sections, not controls, and let the page be a stack of them. Give sections an explicit breakpoint axis with values named after your real breakpoints. Absorb content variety through slots and instance swaps so the variant budget stays available for breakpoints. Check what your CMS can author before designing the component, because that is the binding constraint. Keep the number of breakpoint values to the number of genuinely different compositions, usually two or three rather than the five or six in your CSS.

**Warning signs**, which are easier to act on than principles. Designers detaching instances to make them fit means the component is not responsive and no variant will fix it. A variant grid past one screen means some axes belong in properties or modes. A mobile and desktop variant differing only in padding and font size means one should be deleted and the values bound to a scale mode. A marketing section with no breakpoint variants, where every page has a detached mobile version, means the axis was needed and skipped.

And one more, which is where Part One ends and Part Two begins: a product library that has started growing components called Hero and Marquee. That is not a breakpoint problem. Nothing in Part One will fix it.

---

# Part Two: Seams

## Why this is a different question

It is tempting to treat "should the native app have its own library" as the far end of the responsive spectrum, one more step after tablet. It isn't.

The clearest way to see this is that companies routinely split along seams with no width component at all. Adobe runs two design systems for two surfaces that are both desktop-and-mobile web. Atlassian has a brand design system created by marketing sitting alongside the product system. Neither split is about pixels, and no amount of auto layout would have prevented either.

So the real question is: what property of a surface makes it expensive to keep in the same library as another surface? Once that is answered, web-versus-native falls out as one case among several, and the vocabulary drift noticed at the end of Part One turns out to be the most reliable early symptom.

## Chapter 6: What actually earns a split

Working backwards from the systems that have split and the systems that have not, the same three properties keep appearing on the splitting side, and a different three on the other.

![Seven properties of a surface, each marked as either justifying a library split or belonging in tokens and governance](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Filled markers on the left justify a separate component library. Hollow markers on the right belong in token modes or in governance. Release cadence sits between the two and rarely decides the question alone.*

**Rendering runtime** is the most cited. Spotify's Encore is explicit: Encore Web serves anything built with web technology, which they list as web apps, websites, the desktop client and, in a line I enjoy, the fridge app. Encore Mobile serves mobile technology. The seam is the runtime, not the product and not the screen. Microsoft Fluent 2 splits its Core UI kits into Web, iOS and Android for the same reason. Ant Design keeps `antd` and Ant Design Mobile as separate projects, and when someone proposed merging them the counter-argument was the honest one: some components only make sense on one platform, and a mobile NavBar is useless on a desktop site.

**Authoring environment** is the most under-discussed and, on the evidence, just as strong. Adobe's Consonant exists because Adobe.com is authored in a CMS by content designers and agencies rather than assembled by engineers, and the one-to-one mapping between design template and content block from Part One's Chapter 3 is what makes those two populations able to work in parallel. IBM's marketing system carries the same constraint. When the people consuming your library are content authors rather than developers, the library needs a different vocabulary, and forcing that vocabulary into a product library helps nobody.

**Component vocabulary** is a consequence of the first two, but it is the easiest signal to spot, and it is the one Part One left you with. A product library has Button, Select, Table. A marketing library has Marquee, Leadspace, Content Block, FLEGO. When one library contains both vocabularies, it is two libraries in a trenchcoat.

On the other side of the line:

**Different visual style is not a split.** That is what token modes are for. Atlassian's marketing typeface is not the product interface typeface, and that difference lives in the type tokens, not in a duplicated component set.

**Different team is not a split either.** It is a governance question. Splitting the library to match the org chart produces two libraries that must be kept in parity forever, which is a bigger tax than a shared library with clear ownership.

**Different brand is a token split, not a component split.** This is what Figma's extended collections, shipped at Schema 2025 in October 2025, exist for, and they are Enterprise-gated.

**Release cadence sits in the middle**, which is why it gets its own marker. Nathan Curtis (commentary) has observed that federated native libraries tend to lag central releases by months or quarters. That divergence is real and argues for separately publishable libraries, but it argues equally well for a shared library with staged adoption, so it rarely decides the question alone.

## Chapter 7: The layer underneath never splits

Whatever the components do, the tier beneath them is shared. This is the strongest convergence in the evidence base, and unusually it is convergence across genuinely different constraints rather than one idea echoed.

![Three library stacks, Spotify, Adobe and IBM, each with component libraries above a shared foundation layer](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Spotify splits by runtime, Adobe by authoring environment, IBM runs three levels. The seam differs; the shared tier underneath does not.*

Spotify's Encore Foundation holds colour, type styles, motion, spacing, and the writing and accessibility guidelines, and using it is described as the minimum bar for every Spotify product. Microsoft's Fluent design language file holds colour, stroke width, corner radius, spacing and size tokens for web and mobile alike. Adobe's Consonant sits on top of Spectrum and inherits its corner radii, type hierarchy and button styling. IBM runs three levels, with Carbon for IBM.com built on foundations from both Carbon and the IBM Design Language. Atlassian's local systems, the marketing one included, inherit foundations from the central system.

Three of those are runtime splits, one is a purpose split, and they produce the same shape. That is the part to copy, and it is the same layer Part One's Chapter 2 asked you to build for scale modes. It is doing double duty: absorbing width variation within a surface, and absorbing platform variation across surfaces. Everything else in this guide can be decided per surface. This cannot.

The practical benefit is that the expensive question, whether two things are really the same, gets answered once in the tokens instead of repeatedly and inconsistently in every component. The practical cost, well documented in Figma's forums, is that modes apply per collection, so switching a frame to a different platform or scale can mean setting the mode more than once. There is no clean fix today.

## Chapter 8: What splitting costs

The systems that split are candid about the bill, and the most useful evidence is a documented reversal.

Spotify introduced Encore in 2019 as two segments: a very flexible Consumer Mobile catalogue and a broader Web system. By 2022 their own assessment was that the pendulum had swung too far toward flexibility and a recalibration was needed. They assembled a dedicated team to build cross-platform components and introduced a cross-platform naming system, so updates could happen at the cross-platform level and flow outward into the subsystems. Note what they did *not* do: they did not merge the libraries. They kept the runtime seam and fixed the drift by pulling shared decisions up into the foundation and unifying naming across the two.

That is the general lesson. The cost of splitting is not the second file, it is parity, and parity is bought with shared naming and a shared foundation rather than with merging.

The other cost is ambiguity about ownership. Atlassian describes this as unfinished work, asking openly what belongs in which system and how local systems should be governed. Their framing of a "pervasive API", where a consumer should not have to care which team maintains a component as long as they compose cleanly, is the right target and an honest admission they had not reached it.

HMRC supplies the counterweight, and it is the only case here with a user-facing argument rather than an organisational one. Building the GOV.UK app, they found that a system written for web pages left them without guidance wherever GOV.UK conventions and native operating system conventions diverged, and the app drifted as a result. Their example is precise: interactive rows where the web used text links. The conclusion, that responsiveness alone does not always solve it, is the best single sentence in this material, because it names what library structure is downstream of. They built a separate mobile design system extending GOV.UK and later open-sourced it with its iOS and Android component libraries.

The systems that did not split are not confused, they are correctly scoped. Shopify Polaris covers the admin and nothing else, with responsiveness handled in code through container queries. IBM's core Carbon keeps one library across four themes using modes. Salesforce ships a single web component library and treats touch versus cursor as density rather than platform. And Spotify's Encore Web serves both websites and web apps: Spotify does not split marketing from product, because the runtime and the authoring environment are the same. That is a genuine counter-example to Adobe and IBM, and it holds up.

## Chapter 9: A structure to start from

![A four-layer structure with foundations at the base, then shared icons, then three component libraries, then consuming files](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Read bottom up. Add a component library only for a surface that has earned one; a webview app has not.*

Read it bottom up. Foundations holds variables and no components, with a primitive collection, a semantic collection, and a scale or density collection whose modes match real device tiers. Icons and typography sit above as their own shared libraries, because duplicating those is the fastest route to two systems that no longer look related. Then component libraries, one per surface that has earned it.

Which surfaces earn it depends on your seams. A responsive web product alone needs one. A web product plus a genuinely native app needs two. Add a CMS-authored marketing site and you have three, and the third will have a different vocabulary by design. A webview app earns nothing; that is a breakpoint, and Part One covers it.

**Thresholds that change the answer.** If the native app is a wrapper, do not split. If the marketing site is a handful of pages authored by the same designers who build the product, do not split; make a page templates file that consumes the product library. If two libraries contain components identical except for the file they live in, the split has outrun its justification and those components belong in the shared tier. If you are on Enterprise and the driver is brand rather than surface, use extended collections and do not split components at all.

**Warning signs.** Nobody can say which library owns a component: a governance gap, and no file structure fixes it. The same fix landing twice, once per library: the divergence was never real, pull it down into foundations. A marketing team quietly maintaining a detached copy of the product library: the vocabulary has diverged and the split is overdue. Two libraries whose components share a name but not an API: the parity failure Spotify addressed with cross-platform naming, and worth addressing the same way.

---

# A closing thought

Much of the current advice on both questions is downstream of tooling that changed recently. Polaris chose a variant toggle in 2022 because variables did not exist. Teams built breakpoint grids because four modes per collection could not cover seven breakpoints, a limit that moved in October 2025. Figma Sites made per-breakpoint art direction a first-class operation in 2025. Extended collections arrived only months ago. Every system in this evidence base has migrated something.

The split-or-not question, meanwhile, tends to get argued as though it were a matter of discipline, where a stronger team would keep everything in one place. The evidence does not support that. Splitting is not a failure of will, it is a response to a seam that already exists in the runtime or the authoring environment, and pretending it is not there just moves the cost onto whoever uses the library. What distinguishes the systems that handle it well is that they split components and share everything underneath, and that when the halves drift they fix the shared layer rather than merging. Spotify's recalibration is the clearest worked example and is worth more than the tally of who split and who didn't.

One caveat about that tally. Fluent, Primer, Carbon, Atlassian, Polaris and GitLab are Western corporate systems of the same era, drawing on an overlapping talent pool and publishing into the same conference circuit. Six of them agreeing is closer to one idea with five echoes than to six independent confirmations. The convergences worth weighting are the ones from different constraint worlds: Spotify splitting by runtime while Adobe splits by authoring environment, the Chinese systems splitting for mini-program and React Native ecosystem reasons that have nothing to do with Figma, and HMRC arriving at a split from statutory accessibility requirements and user research.

Which leads to the thing worth saying plainly about both parts. None of this rests on user research. No system in this set published evidence that any of these structural choices affected the people using their products. HMRC comes closest, and even there the finding is about designers lacking guidance rather than measured user outcomes. These are decisions about maintenance cost and the ergonomics of a design tool, which is a perfectly good basis for a decision as long as nobody dresses it up as something else.

So the useful posture is not finding the correct structure but keeping the cost of changing it low. Name things so they can be renamed, keep the token layer separable from the components, and treat any current answer as provisional.

## Appendix: State of play, August 2026

Worth re-verifying before relying on any of it.

Variable mode limits changed on 28 October 2025 to 10 per collection on Professional and 20 on Organization. Extended collections, the mechanism for brand-level token variation without duplicating libraries, shipped at Schema 2025 in October 2025 and are Enterprise-gated. Figma Sites remains in open beta, having launched at Config 2025; Sites CMS entered public beta on 20 November 2025, which matters for anyone considering a marketing library that lives in Figma end to end. The breakpoint-to-variant-name matching remains a Sites feature with no sign of reaching ordinary design files. Config 2026 in June 2026 launched Code Layers, Motion, shaders and an expanded agent, none of which touched either decision space, which is itself worth knowing. Code Connect's framework-specific parsers stop receiving updates on 17 August 2026, with template files becoming the maintained path.
